title: Gratitude
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 93 of the Blue Cliff Record, where a monk asks about giving thanks at lunch and Daguang answers by dancing, along with the earlier Case 74 on Jinniu's rice pail. Before that, Nomon sets a rain-soaked Zen backpacking trip on Mount Baker beside a day at a Volkswagen dealership, where desire for a flood-damaged 2012 Golf TDI meets bad news. Drawing on Kate's talk about fearful doubt, Nomon asks whether gratitude can reach difficult states of mind, then turns to play, recalling Kate's story of a two-year-old bouncing a ball. The monk who copies Daguang's dance is called a stupid fox, so each person must find a dance of their own.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
One of the interesting aspects of being late, like I did tonight, is actually I really don't know who's here.
Because that is a great part of Zen practice.
When we're practicing formally in the Zen, though, just to be within ourselves and just kind of looking forward and down.
And so I hadn't really looked around.
Then the service started and I heard Matt's voice, and then I started sort of catching little glimpses of other people.
So anyway, it's nice to see you.
And then Cary, or Sue, Sue Cary was sitting over there.
I haven't seen her in a long time.
So anyway, it's an interesting life, isn't it?
So many different situations happen and somehow we show up in the middle of it all.
So I just want to share a few contrasting experiences that I've had lately and say a few words of appreciation for Kate's talk from last week.
And if you weren't here, you can listen to that on the website and start to develop a new theme.
I have an idea for a new theme: what happens?
So on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, with three of our Sangamates, I was high in the mountains, the Cascade Mountains on the flanks of Mount Baker.
We hiked slowly up a very gradual trail, starting in kind of a thick hemlock forest, western hemlock forest, big hemlocks, probably five, eighty years old.
And then gradually they thinned out and the trees changed and things opened up, and there was a threat of rain.
The rain was in the forecast, and as you know, rain can be kind of like intense in the mountains, but it wasn't raining and we were happy and we got a good start.
We had lunch and the sunshine.
Then after lunch, it suddenly got very cloudy very quickly and then it did rain, and it rained so hard.
And so it's like it was suddenly like this whole different world.
There was the sunny world of the mountains.
And we have this idea that there's like the mountains, which is like one thing, and then there's these overlays, you know, weather and people and conditions, right?
But actually I didn't really feel that way.
I felt like, wow, in a whole different world, you know, a world of cold and water and noise, and there was thunder and lightning.
And when we take a break, all we could really do is to stand there with our arms down.
If you put your arms up, the water would run in your sleeves.
You stand there, arms down, watching the water just kind of go down, down, down, down, down.
And that's where some of it's getting in and you're getting water, and then eventually the next day it was just quiet and misty or in a cloud, you know, life in a cloud.
On these Zen backpacking hikes, Bob Penny has kind of concocted a really nice way to integrate Zen practice and backpacking.
We hike silently and we stop and we do chanting and we get up early and do meditation in this little kind of forest service sort of shelter.
That's where we go, and it's just very quiet and beautiful.
And I just found myself just more than usual with a sort of sense of like drinking it in, you know, just like just drinking in that place.
Here's this beautiful place, you know, fifty miles from here or something like that, is the Crow Fry.
It's not that far.
That's like a whole other world, you know, a changeable world to be sure.
And the last day, one of the people with us, Nick—I forget his last name, Young Nick—he is a fairly new backpacker, it turns out.
He probably won't be too embarrassed if I rat him out a little bit.
He said, "Yeah, sure, I've been backpacking before."
It turns out that man, he and his girlfriend had hiked to her land in the Kitsap Peninsula, which is like flat and spent the night.
So he wasn't super prepared and it was all kind of new to him and a little bit intense and overwhelming.
And this whole time, the first couple of days, rain and his not quite adequate backpacking, you know, clothing was soaked to the skin.
And then just clouds, you can't see anything.
And then the last day it did, it opened up.
We woke up that morning, there's Mount Baker.
So that was nice.
I was happy to get to be there while he took that in.
He's a pretty quiet guy.
He was a subtle kind of guy.
And then today I was in a big city full of cars and crowds and people on their cell phones.
And I was in the dealership, a Volkswagen dealership, very busy, big city dealership, where like when you check in your car, there's like this like assembly line system.
Like there's a guy who receives your car and drives it off somewhere, vanishes instantly.
And then there's this line of receptionists who check you in.
And it's all very official and very fast moving.
And I'm like, "Wow, you know, this is like all another human expression."
And I thought the hemlock trees we were hiking through on Friday existed long before any of this was even like invented.
I mean, there aren't no cars or concrete buildings or anything like that.
I guess concrete, the Romans invented, but you know, no Seattle skyscraper buildings.
And I was there on the horns of desire, too.
I had kind of fallen in love.
I need a car.
I need a new car because I'm getting more and more mindfulness work sort of scattered around working for these different medical centers, working with doctors.
And I've had our one car away too much.
And Janice like getting a little tired of like she gets up one day and needs to go shopping or take Walker somewhere, and there's like no cars to get a car.
And so it's been interesting car shopping.
And I used to be like somewhat immune to this.
I thought, "Just get a cheap Honda.
It doesn't matter.
It's just a car.
Who cares?"
But I'm very triggered.
And I really want a 2012 Volkswagen Golf TDI.
I love that car.
I just do.
I'm hopelessly in love with this car.
It's embarrassing.
You're all going to revoke your membership when you leave.
Buddhism doesn't seem to work.
And so I found one at a very good price from a private guy who was selling his 2012 Volkswagen Golf TDI, 18,000 miles, practically brand new.
But it had been in a small freshwater flood.
He said it was a very small flood, and my desire did not allow me to realize it was a bad idea.
So I spent Monday going down there checking it out.
I went back today and he's in Bellevue, but there's no appointments at the dealer in Bellevue.
So the car had to get to Seattle, and there's like so much traffic, and we're going back and forth across.
I want to cross the 520 bridge twice today.
And finally we get to the dealer.
And I thought the dealer had said if you bring it by 9:30, we'll look at it right away.
But the dealer is like, "What the hell are you talking about?
There's 30 cars ahead of you."
It's going to be like four o'clock.
And I'm like, "Oh, it's a Zen night."
So finally the dealer comes back with a completely logical conclusion that they looked under the dash and was otherwise immaculately beautiful.
It was kind of like a midnight blue, beautiful.
I've never had a nice car really.
And anyway, naturally they looked under the dash and they said, "Well, the water line was clearly up to the base of the windshield and all the components show signs of rust.
I'm a real idiot to buy this car."
And it's so interesting how it is for you when you take in news that is not what you want to hear.
You know what I mean?
Like the mind quickly starts spinning up like, "They're wrong.
No, no, they can't be wrong.
There's some way that I can ignore this information.
That's it.
You know, I'll get lucky."
I get lucky.
You know, it works now, but it's like, you know, it's like a time bomb.
Anyway, so I was really in one hand mortified to be in Seattle messing with cars when I should be here.
Eventually we kind of got the car back to the owner and through much.
Oh, then it was like five o'clock.
I thought, "Okay, there's still a chance.
Two hours to go.
You just need to get this car back to Bellevue, drive home without stopping."
And then we looked not quite out the window, but you had to kind of go up the hill a little bit.
We looked down on the I-5, and it's like, you know, just, you know.
So I went from guilty to horrified to actually just appreciative, just knowing that I wasn't going to be on time.
And that was actually okay.
The practice would happen quite beautifully, as it clearly is.
And I'd get there when I could.
And then I kind of let go of the whole thing.
Maybe I won't make it at all.
But Jenna was with me and we had the car pull away in our favor.
Here we are.
So anyway, what a funny life this is.
Hemlock forests and rain and desire and letting go and good news and bad news happening all the time.
Things that you aren't supposed to care about, you care about.
Things that you don't care about, you should.
Who knows how it goes.
I did really appreciate Kate's talk last week, which is somehow connected to my little sketch there.

Because she was really talking about, you know, how is it to be in the middle of this mind, you know, this heart and mind, which we got somehow the information, or maybe we made it up, that we could control.
And so she's been trying to kind of negotiate her way through a mind full of the confusions and doubts that all of our minds generate or seem to embody at times.
And she talked about working with the five hindrances.
And I have trouble remembering all four because they're two pairs that are pretty similar.
And I figured out a shorthand way to remember the five hindrances.
It's basically trying too hard or being lazy or doubting that the whole thing is worth bothering with.
So it's kind of like my thumbnail sketch of the five hindrances.

And Kate talked particularly about doubt and the kind of, there are different flavors of doubt, but she seemed to be particularly talking about the doubt that's really laced with fear, which is such a powerful emotion.
That feeling of being fragile and inadequate, doubting you're up for this task of, you know, practice, but maybe even more fundamentally doubting that we're up for this task of just being a person.
What if we're not up for it?
It's frightening.
And the way that when that kind of vibration, that kind of feeling catches hold in your mind, it's not always there, but when it is, how easily it distorts our perception and thinking.
She talked about how this kind of fearful doubt causes us to overgeneralize.
One thing goes wrong and then it seems like everything's going wrong.
"I'm never going to find a 2012 company."
And she spoke so eloquently about the really true fact, I think, that the only way forward is through.
That we cannot try to ignore or do an end run or figure out a fix to the mind that can be so caught with doubt and fear.
We have to enter into it.
And she talked about in the Christian tradition, the idea of the dark night of the soul and brought up some wonderful Christian monastics.
I think the interesting thing, though, is that we do have some we can't we cannot control our mind.
This is clear.
We can practice with the mind.
We can respond to the mind.
And occasionally we snap out of whatever it is we're stuck in.
And that's kind of nice.
So I have actually let go of Alex Bebik's 2012 Golf TDI.
He consulted somebody else.
He's a good guy.
He wasn't trying to trick me, actually.
He didn't realize, you know, that there was more damage and he took it off Craig's listings and tried to fix it.
But anyway, so we have a choice here, though, in how we relate to and work with the difficult states of mind.
I think it could be if we engage with it in a creative way, somewhat skillful way, supported by a practice, then it can be the dark night of the soul.
But the soul is there, right?
This is a powerful opportunity to learn and grow, to breathe our way through the dark night of the soul.
Or it can just be a dark night.
Or it can just be misery.
So how do we show up when we're caught by desire, by doubt, overwhelmed by beauty?
It's not so easy to show up.
I think our training helps our training and stability and acceptance.
Then it comes down to some very, very simple moment-by-moment practices that are not so elaborate, like bringing the mind back to the breath and body.
This is a deep training.
We can't have to underestimate the power of something that's that simple and deep, just returning to the present.
But that plants the seeds or develops the muscles, or however you want to think about it.
Every way we try to talk about the mind and working with the mind is always metaphor, right?
It's always approximate.
It's always a little bit rough.
The mind is much more complicated than our language, than our plans, than our car choices.
Maybe it comes down to sort of gradually cultivating a kind of a mindset, a mindset that it's going to be worth it.
It's going to be worth showing up to the joys and to the misery, to the blessings, to the horrors.
That it's really worth showing up, and then cultivating and developing that mindset will make that skillfulness of engagement available to us when the night gets dark.
We'll feel the soul that is there.
Anyway, a little riff off Kate's talk, but you should listen to her actual talk.
It wasn't really exactly what I said, even kind of, but just what I appreciated about it.

As you know, I'm increasingly interested in connections between sort of traditional Buddhist understanding, or who knows if anything we're doing is exactly traditional—everything's interpreted and changing over time—but Buddhist understanding will say connections between Buddhist understanding and also current science and psychology and neuroscience and philosophy and poetry.
And just the way so much seems to be sort of meeting right now in a way that's really beautiful and actually really helpful.
One of the things that I've been reading a bit about the science of happiness is what actually makes us happy.
Are we looking for happiness in all the wrong places?

One of the things that they consistently find in their studies—and one could take issues with their studies, I'm sure, like how can you exactly define or measure happiness—is there's a strong connection between gratitude and happiness.
Seems to be the strongest correlate of the various things they're looking at that might really support lasting and deep happiness or joy.
Happiness is a frivolous sounding word to you.
You can substitute joy or you to me or something if you're into Greek philosophy.
I was thinking it's pretty reasonably easy.
For one thing, I think gratitude is basically we forget about gratitude, and that's kind of part of how we're wired up, right?
Gratitude gets occluded or crowded out by desire or doubt or any number of things.
But it's actually reasonably possible to cultivate gratitude for the things that we like and appreciate.
It's not actually that hard.
You need a little training, and you got to remind yourself, and it helps to have friends and a practice.
But it's not that hard to actually pause from time to time and really appreciate and really feel the wonderful things that we have been given.
And there's so many, right?
There's so much that we can appreciate, even if there are also some things that the mind quickly goes to that are like, you know, really terrible.
But if we think about it, slow down a little bit, we can list off quite a few things that we're very grateful for that are truly wonderful, really fantastic.
So what are you grateful for?
Think about it for a minute.
Some of these things we take for granted, so we have to remember to actually have like be healthy enough to walk.
That's pretty great.
There we all have friends and family.
I'm so grateful to the mountains today and nature, and still am, you know, I kind of feel it's more with me than other times.
You can be grateful maybe for having good work to do in the world that actually helps, that makes a difference in the world.
So many things we can be grateful for.
But all this, inspired by Kate's talk about doubt and my sort of watching my own crazy mind, what I wonder about is can we learn?
Can we develop this kind of mindset that makes it more possible to be grateful also for the things that we don't like, the things that are difficult, the difficult emotions?
Kate reminded us of the Sanskrit term *Clashia*, the defilements, all the ways that the mind gets somewhere.
I remember it popped into my mind the etymology of that word, *Clashia*, Sanskrit word *Clashia*.
There's a similar one in polyglot, and the etymology means something like covering the thoughts.
There's a way that our mind kind of covers itself up, or like the sort of, you know, Buddhism, the basic operating idea is fundamentally, there's good stuff here.
Fundamentally, we are, in fact, Buddha, but it gets covered up, you know.
So the *clashas* are these little coverings, you know.
So can we actually become grateful that we know this, that we can feel this, that we can feel these coverings and these defilements and these confusions and this anger?
Can we be grateful to be in a world that's got problems, you know?
Why would we be grateful for that?
Because we want to be able to engage.
We want to be able to engage in a way that has actually some happiness in it.
Not that we're going to just sort of, you know, not worry about it, what me worry, but to be grateful that we have this opportunity to serve and to help.
And can we be grateful when doubt arises?
Maybe doubt's arising in you right now, hearing that thought, you know, grateful for the troubles in the world.
Can we be grateful for doubt?
Can we turn the mind towards curiosity, towards appreciation, no matter what's here?
Because what's here is what's actually here.
I mean, this is the only life we get, so I don't have my.
And so the reason I was so stuck in that car is because I had a fantasy of how happy it would be to be driving down the road in my 2012 Golf TDI.
It would be so nice.
I don't get that, you know.
But it's not the reality of the actual car.
It was my fantasy of it, my thought coverings.
Can we be curious and interested in all this that our minds do, that everyone's minds do, that the actions that flow from our human minds do?
Some of it's so wonderful, some of it horrible.
And there can be a great salve.
So this is, I'm getting my theme here.
This is the kind of space that opens up when the doubt drops away.
I appreciate about Kate's talk when she was talking about her two-year-old friend.
Kate was telling a story that she was visiting with a friend who's a new mom, and the friend's two-year-old was bouncing a ball with total concentration and delight.
Not to put words in Kate's mouth, but more or less the doubt is gone.
It's just the ball and bouncing.
You know how it's like a little bit unpredictable which way it's going to bounce, kind of imagining this kid and the miracle of hands and arms and responding and time and space and movement.
I mean, it's amazing, you know.
And you were like, yeah, it's just a ball.
It's amazing.
So what I'm getting interested in is play, is play.
This all seems so serious, right?
Doubt is serious.
Troubles of the world are serious.
We take ourselves seriously in serious trouble when others are rude to us or don't understand us or don't give us everything we think that we deserve from them in this particular moment.
How are they going to know?
But they should.
When bad news comes, it's so serious.
I mean, it was actually, I have to admit, a crushing blow that the components beneath the dashboard were corroded.
It felt very serious, you know, for at least a little minute there, well, maybe fifteen at least.
I had to sit down, actually.
Jan, let's just sit down.
The process is like a death in the family.
Are you sitting down?
So we get so serious.
So can we meet seriousness, you know, with appropriate response, for sure.
Sometimes it's very helpful to be to meet serious with seriousness.
But how about play?
Instead of just like trying to work with all these problems, all these challenges, can we play with them?
And so I want to end with a Zen story that we'll try to unpack a little more another time, Case 93 of the Blue Cliff Record.
The copy I had on hand uses the Japanese voicings of the names.
Mostly now we use Chinese, so I'll look up later the Japanese names or the Chinese names so they might be more familiar from other stories.
Case is called Taiko Dances.
Here's the story: A monk asked Taiko, Choke, a teacher, another monk.
Choke said that is exactly like giving thanks at lunch.
What did he mean?
Taiko danced.
The monk made a deep bow.
But then Taiko said, what have you seen that makes you bow like that?
So the monk danced.
And Taiko was unimpressed.
He said, you stupid fox.
It turns out a fox means like an imitator, a trick, a tricker, an imitator.
So just imitating Taiko's dancing, wasn't it?
A monk asked Taiko, Choke said that's exactly like giving thanks at lunch.
What did he mean?
So Taiko just danced.
The monk made a deep bow.
Taiko said, what have you seen that makes you bow like that?
The monk danced.
Taiko said, you stupid fox.
I don't know, I guess I felt like a stupid fox today or something.
This is actually also, there also is a reference here to another story.
So I'll redo that story and then I'll stop and maybe I'll put some stuff in the email too.
And next time I get to go talk we can talk about these stories.
There's an earlier story that is connected to giving thanks at lunch.
So the Choke reference is probably a reference to this story, Case 74 from the same collection.
It's called King Yu's Rice Bucket.

At each meal, Master King Yu himself, it's like the teacher, Master King himself would bring the rice bucket to the front of the Zen hall and dance and laugh loudly calling, "Dear Bodhisattvas, come and eat your rice."
And a monk asked Choke, it's the same Choke, an ancient worthy said, "Dear Bodhisattvas, come and eat rice."
What does this mean?
Choke said that's exactly like praising and giving thanks to the rice.
So of course, if you're spending time in monasteries, there's not a lot of dancing.
It's a pretty serious business, pretty quiet, pretty tiring.
The monks and nuns are mostly like pretty physically tired.
You know, sometimes there's some lightness and joy for sure, but it's a grueling thing.
And so here we have a couple of cases among the many Zen stories about gratitude and dancing, but that it's not so simple.
It's just flapping our limbs around.
It's not just so simple as making a joke.
It's not just so simple as, "Oh, I heard about Kate's boy, I'm going to get my ball, oh, ball therapy."
That's it.
You know, it's not about imitating.

It's each of us finding our way, finding our dance, finding our way to play, finding our way to laugh at ourselves when we get caught, finding our way to respond and wake up again, finding our way to be without and to be with joy.
So hopefully that was more or less coherent.
It was mostly written while I was waiting for the mechanic, not in the mechanic's office, but we went to a nice place at the university.
Had a nice little lunch, so it wasn't all bad.
